newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's MRTA rebel attack sparks fire, seven hurt.
newsitem.headline: Peru's MRTA rebel attack sparks fire, seven hurt.

text.p: Marxist rebels burst into a textile factory in Lima on Saturday, shouting slogans and tossing grenades, sparking a fire that injured at least seven firefighters, authorities said.
"It's a terrorist attack. They used hand grenades," police bomb squad officer Carlos Samaniego told Reuters.

Peruvian anti-terrorist police said the attack was carried out by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the same organisation that has held 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima for 88 days.

On Saturday afternoon, heavily armed rebels entered the wool-products factory in the working class La Victoria district and shouted MRTA slogans before the fire broke out, police quoted witnesses as saying.
They also said authorities found MRTA slogans painted on the outside walls of the building.
"They threw the grenades as they shouted their slogans," said Samaniego. Fire officials said seven firefighters were hurt in the fire but none seriously.
"They identified themselves as MRTA. There were eight to 10 people and they tied up the workers," factory owner Andres Villaran told local radio.

The Lima hostage crisis sparked a new police shakeup as the heads of police special operations directorate (DINOES) and its tactical operations unit (SUAT) were transferred for poor handling of the siege.

An Interior Ministry source said DINOES head Col. Julio Santillan Valdivia and SUAT chief Col. Juan Carlos Mejia Leon were moved to desk jobs in the police Inspector General's Office, partly for leaking information to the news media.

"They were transferred due to the closeness they have with reporters in the handling of information," said the source, who spoke on condition of anonymity. "There were no secrets because everything was known."
President Alberto Fujimori in the early days of the crisis replaced Peru's two top security chiefs, including the head of anti-terrorist police DINCOTE, who were among the hostages.
The government also has several times clashed with the foreign news media since Dec. 17, 1996, when about 20 MRTA rebels stormed the compound during a cocktail party.

A Japanese reporter was expelled from Peru in January after sneaking into the residence to interview rebel chief Nestor Cerpa and, more recently, a foreign cameraman fled the country, citing veiled threats by Peru's intelligence service after he spoke by radio with rebels in the compound.
The cameraman left last week after hostage-takers broke off talks with the government, saying security forces were digging a tunnel to storm the mansion and rescue the hostages.
Fujimori on Saturday scrapped a trip to Bolivia, whose envoy to Lima is one of the hostages but he did not give a reason for the cancellation.

A government spokeswoman said Fujimori has put off to next week the trip to La Paz to meet with Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada, whose ambassador was reportedly showing signs of emotional breakdown as a hostage.

Earlier this week, La Paz's ambassador Jorge Gumucio quarreled with an MRTA rebel inside the compound, in the most serious episode of its kind known to have happened during the siege, a police source said.
The rebel threatened Gumucio with a gun before other hostages intervened to calm him, the source said.
Peruvian media said Gumucio suffered an attack of hysteria but La Paz officials said the ambassador reacted calmly when provoked by the rebel's "offensive" statements about Bolivia.

There have been frequent appeals on health grounds for the release of Gumucio, who is diabetic and has a history of heart and blood pressure problems. But the rebels have held on to the only hostage from a country other than Peru and Japan in the hope of exchanging him for MRTA members jailed in Bolivia.

The MRTA seized hundreds of hostages when it stormed the Japanese diplomatic compound and continued to hold its most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother Pedro, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.

The rebels' main demand was the release of about 400 jailed comrades, nearly all of them in Peru. Fujimori publicly rejected the demand but speculation arose recently that the government was privately considering some minor releases.
